record.original_question: For the hypergraphic planted clique (HPC) detection problem, where one must distinguish an Erdős-Rényi d-hypergraph G_d(N, 1/2) from a planted-clique alternative G_d(N, 1/2, κ) formed by choosing κ vertices uniformly at random and connecting every hyperedge whose vertices all lie in that planted set, what is the sharp threshold on the clique size κ at which polynomial-time singular-value-decomposition-based detection on a matricization or unfolding of the adjacency tensor succeeds, and is there some other polynomial-time algorithm that can solve HPC detection for κ below that SVD threshold?

evidence.quote:
We deﬁne Gd pN, 1{2, κq as the hypergraphic planted clique (HPC) model with the clique size
κ. To generate G „ Gd pN, 1{2, κq, we sample a random hypergraph from Gd pN, 1{2q, pick
κ vertices uniformly at random from rN s, denote them as K, and connect all hyperedges
e if all vertices of e are in K. The hypergraphic planted clique detection (HPC) can be
formulated as the following hypothesis testing problem:
                   H0 : G „ Gd pN, 1{2q    v.s. H1 : G „ Gd pN, 1{2, κq .                 (1)

Challenge 1 Can we establish the sharp limit of κ to guarantee that HPC can be solved by
SVD on the matricization/unfolding of A? Is it possible to develop another polynomial-time
algorithm for HPC that works below this limit?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer d ≥ 3. For a positive integer N, let [N] = {1, …, N}. The Erdős–Rényi d-uniform hypergraph G_d(N, 1/2) is the random hypergraph on vertex set [N] in which each of the C(N,d) possible d-element hyperedges is included independently with probability 1/2. The hypergraphic planted clique model G_d(N, 1/2, κ), with clique size κ ∈ {1, …, N}, is generated as follows: first sample G ~ G_d(N, 1/2); then pick a subset K ⊂ [N] with |K| = κ uniformly at random; then add (or keep) every d-element hyperedge whose vertices all lie in K. The hypergraphic planted clique (HPC) detection problem is the hypothesis testing problem

  H0: G ~ G_d(N, 1/2)   versus   H1: G ~ G_d(N, 1/2, κ),

with the goal of finding a test whose Type-I plus Type-II error probability tends to 0 as N → ∞.

Encode the hypergraph by its symmetric d-th order adjacency tensor A ∈ {0,1}^{N×N×…×N}. For an integer 1 ≤ k ≤ d−1, the (k, d−k)-matricization (unfolding) of A is the N^k × N^{d−k} matrix M_k(A) obtained by grouping the first k tensor indices into rows and the remaining d−k indices into columns. A "SVD-based detector on a matricization/unfolding of A" is any test that thresholds the leading singular value of M_k(A) (for some k) after appropriate centering.

Determine the following:

(a) Identify the sharp threshold function κ*(N, d) such that for κ ≫ κ*(N, d) some SVD-based test on a matricization/unfolding of A solves HPC detection (errors → 0), while for κ ≪ κ*(N, d) every such SVD-based test fails (errors → 1).

(b) Decide whether there exists a polynomial-time algorithm (not necessarily based on the SVD of a matricization) that solves HPC detection for some κ asymptotically below the threshold in (a).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem was posed as an open problem in 2020. A 2026 work studies spectral detection/recovery for planted cliques in hypergraphs and shows a spectral norm test is asymptotically powerful at the √N scale, but does not claim to have closed the SVD-vs-other-polynomial-time gap or to have resolved the open question. No source clearly establishes the sharp SVD matricization threshold together with a polynomial-time algorithm beating it, so the problem appears still open.

status_evidence.title: Open Problem: Average-Case Hardness of Hypergraphic Planted Clique Detection
status_evidence.snippet: Open problem on average-case hardness of HPC detection.
status_evidence.claim: The HPC detection threshold and polynomial-time algorithmic frontier are stated as an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Planted clique detection and recovery from the hypergraph adjacency matrix
status_evidence.snippet: A spectral norm test is asymptotically powerful at the √n scale; a polynomial-time spectral method based on the leading eigenvector achieves exact recovery at the canonical √n scale.
status_evidence.claim: Recent spectral results match the √N scale typical of SVD methods but do not claim to surpass it via another polynomial-time algorithm.
